Which statement best justifies whether the data support this claim?

choices.text: Since the mean for students who study mostly at night (40) is greater than for students who study mostly in the morning (35), every member of students who study mostly at night must have a higher self-reported focus rating than every member of students who study mostly in the morning.

On average students who study mostly at night had a higher self-reported focus rating (mean 40 vs 35), so the data support a typical difference; but because both SDs are about 14, the distributions overlap substantially, so the data do not support a claim that students who study mostly at night are always higher.
These results prove that students who study mostly at night will always outperform students who study mostly in the morning on self-reported focus rating in any future study or population.
Because students who study mostly at night had a higher mean self-reported focus rating, being in students who study mostly at night causes a higher self-reported focus rating.

topic_evidence.title: Graphical Representations for One Categorical Variable

stem: After-School Activity Survey: Answer all parts. Show your reasoning and calculations clearly, using standard AP notation and justifying any qualitative claims.
stimulus:
A student council surveyed all 80 students in the tenth grade at Lincoln High School, asking each student to identify the after-school activity in which they participate most.

Table 1: After-School Activity of Tenth-Grade Students
Activity | Number of Students
Sports | 32
Music | 12
Clubs | 20
None | 16

part_prompts.text: Calculate the relative frequency (proportion) of tenth-grade students in each of the four activity categories. Show the division used for at least one category.
Construct a bar graph of the distribution of after-school activity.
Describe the distribution of after-school activity based on the graph, identifying the most and least common activities.
Classify the type of variable recorded (activity), and justify why a bar graph, rather than a histogram, is the appropriate display for this variable.

stem: Carnival Spinner Probabilities: Answer all parts. Show your reasoning and calculations clearly, using standard AP notation and justifying any qualitative claims.
stimulus: A carnival game uses a spinner divided into 8 equally likely sectors: 3 red, 2 blue, 2 green, and 1 yellow. A player spins the spinner once.

part_prompts.text: Calculate the probability that the spinner lands on red or blue.
Calculate the probability that the spinner does not land on green.
Determine whether the events "the spinner lands on red" and "the spinner lands on blue" are mutually exclusive, and justify your answer.
Suppose the player spins the spinner twice, and the spins are independent. Calculate the probability that both spins land on red.

stem: Selecting a Random Sample of Students: Answer all parts. Show your reasoning and calculations clearly, using standard AP notation and justifying any qualitative claims.
stimulus: A school has 400 students enrolled, each assigned a unique ID number from 001 to 400. A researcher wants to select a simple random sample (SRS) of 15 students to survey about cafeteria satisfaction. The researcher has a list of all 400 ID numbers and access to a table of random digits.

part_prompts.text: Explain a complete and correct procedure the researcher could use with the random digit table to select an SRS of 15 students from the 400.
Explain why using this SRS procedure to select students reduces bias compared to only surveying whichever students happen to be in the cafeteria line during 5th period.
Calculate the probability that a particular student, Maria, is included in the sample of 15.

topic_evidence.title: Descriptions for One Quantitative Variable Distributions

stem: Marathon Training Distances: Answer all parts. Show your reasoning and calculations clearly, using standard AP notation and justifying any qualitative claims.
stimulus:
A running coach recorded the weekly training distance (in miles) for 12 runners preparing for a marathon:

18, 22, 24, 25, 26, 28, 28, 29, 31, 33, 35, 61

part_prompts.text: Calculate the mean and the median weekly training distance for these 12 runners. Show your work.
Describe the shape of the distribution and explain how the shape is reflected in the relationship between the mean and median found in part A.

A sports reporter wants to summarize the "typical" weekly training distance for this group. Justify which measure of center (mean or median) is more appropriate to report, and calculate an appropriate measure of spread to accompany your choice.

topic_evidence.title: Graphical Representations of Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable

stem: Tomato Plant Heights: Answer all parts. Show your reasoning and calculations clearly, using standard AP notation and justifying any qualitative claims.
stimulus:
A gardener measured the heights (in cm) of 11 tomato plants grown from the same seed batch. The five-number summary of the heights is given below.

Table 1: Five-Number Summary of Tomato Plant Heights (cm)
Min | Q1 | Median | Q3 | Max
34 | 42 | 48 | 55 | 90

Raw heights (cm): 34, 39, 42, 44, 46, 48, 50, 52, 55, 60, 90.

part_prompts.text: Determine whether the maximum value of 90 cm is an outlier using the 1.5×IQR rule. Show all work.
Construct a modified boxplot for the data that correctly displays the outlier identified in part A.

Describe the shape of the distribution suggested by the five-number summary and boxplot, and explain how the presence of the outlier affects the choice between the mean/standard deviation and the median/IQR for describing center and spread.

topic_evidence.title: Tabular and Graphical Representations for the Distributions of Two Categorical Variables

stem: Streaming Service Preference by Age Group: Answer all parts. Show your reasoning and calculations clearly, using standard AP notation and justifying any qualitative claims.
stimulus:
A media company surveyed 200 randomly selected adults about their preferred streaming service (A, B, or C) and recorded each respondent's age group.

Table 1: Streaming Preference by Age Group
 | Under 30 | 30 and Over | Total
Service A | 48 | 32 | 80
Service B | 24 | 56 | 80
Service C | 8 | 32 | 40
Total | 80 | 120 | 200

part_prompts.text: Calculate the marginal distribution of streaming service preference (overall proportions for A, B, and C).
Calculate the conditional distribution of streaming preference for adults Under 30, and separately for adults 30 and Over.
Compare the two conditional distributions from part B, and use them to determine whether streaming preference and age group appear to be associated.
Calculate the probability that a randomly selected survey respondent is Under 30 and prefers Service C.

stem: Allergy Test Accuracy: Answer all parts. Show your reasoning and calculations clearly, using standard AP notation and justifying any qualitative claims.
stimulus: A clinic uses a screening test for a particular allergy. In the population the clinic serves, 15% of people actually have the allergy. Given that a person has the allergy, the test returns a positive result 92% of the time. Given that a person does not have the allergy, the test incorrectly returns a positive result (false positive) 6% of the time.

part_prompts.text: Using a hypothetical group of 1000 people, fill in a table showing the four possible outcomes (allergy/no allergy crossed with positive/negative test result), with expected counts.
Calculate the probability that a randomly selected person actually has the allergy, given that their test result is positive.
Explain why the probability calculated in part B is much lower than 92%, the test's accuracy rate for people who have the allergy, referencing the context.

stem: Carnival Game Payout: Answer all parts. Show your reasoning and calculations clearly, using standard AP notation and justifying any qualitative claims.
stimulus:
In a carnival game, a player pays $5 to play. The player draws one ball from a bag of 20 numbered balls and wins a prize based on the type of ball drawn.

Table 1: Prize Winnings
Outcome | Number of balls | Winnings (X)
Grand prize | 1 | $50
Medium prize | 4 | $10
Small prize | 5 | $2
No prize | 10 | $0

part_prompts.text: Calculate the expected value of the winnings X for one play of the game.
Interpret the value found in part A in the context of whether the game is fair, given that it costs $5 to play.
Calculate the standard deviation of the winnings X.
Explain what the standard deviation found in part C indicates about the variability of outcomes in this game, compared to a hypothetical game with SD = $2.

stem: Free Throw Shooting: Answer all parts. Show your reasoning and calculations clearly, using standard AP notation and justifying any qualitative claims.
stimulus: A basketball player makes 75% of her free throws, and each attempt can be considered independent of the others. During a game, she attempts 6 free throws. Let X represent the number of free throws she makes.

part_prompts.text: Justify why X, the number of free throws made out of 6 attempts, can be modeled by a binomial random variable.
Calculate the probability that she makes exactly 4 of the 6 free throws.
Calculate the mean and standard deviation of X, the number of free throws made out of 6.

stem: Fertilizer Experiment on Bean Plants: Answer all parts. Show your reasoning and calculations clearly, using standard AP notation and justifying any qualitative claims.
stimulus: A researcher wants to determine whether a new fertilizer increases bean plant yield compared to the standard fertilizer. She has 40 bean plants of the same variety, all similar in initial size, arranged on 4 shelves (10 plants per shelf) at different distances from the greenhouse's light source.

part_prompts.text: Explain how the researcher should use random assignment in this experiment and why it is important.
Describe how the researcher could incorporate blocking into the experimental design using the 4 shelves, and explain the potential benefit of doing so.
Identify the explanatory variable and the response variable in this experiment.
Explain why this study is an experiment rather than an observational study.

stem: Standardized Test Scores: Answer all parts. Show your reasoning and calculations clearly, using standard AP notation and justifying any qualitative claims.
stimulus: Scores on a national standardized test are approximately normally distributed with a mean of 500 and a standard deviation of 90.

part_prompts.text: Calculate the probability that a randomly selected test-taker scores above 650.
Determine the test score that separates the top 10% of test-takers from the rest.
A random sample of 36 test-takers is selected. Calculate the probability that the sample mean score is above 520.

topic_evidence.title: Comparisons of the Distributions for One Quantitative Variable

stem: Comparing Commute Times at Two Offices: Answer all parts. Show your reasoning and calculations clearly, using standard AP notation and justifying any qualitative claims.
stimulus:
A company measured one-way commute times (in minutes) for random samples of employees at its Downtown office and its Suburban office.

Downtown (n=9): 12, 15, 18, 20, 22, 25, 28, 30, 55
Suburban (n=9): 25, 27, 29, 30, 31, 33, 34, 36, 38

part_prompts.text: Calculate the mean and median commute time for each office.
Compare the distributions of commute times at the two offices in context, addressing shape, center, and spread.
Determine whether the value of 55 minutes in the Downtown data is an outlier, using the 1.5×IQR rule.
Explain why the median is a more appropriate measure to use when comparing "typical" commute time between the two offices than the mean.

stem: Mall Survey Bias: Answer all parts. Show your reasoning and calculations clearly, using standard AP notation and justifying any qualitative claims.
stimulus: A shopping mall manager wants to estimate the proportion of all adults in the city who shop online at least once per week. She stands outside a department store on a Tuesday afternoon and surveys the first 100 adults who walk by.

part_prompts.text: Identify the sampling method used in this study.
Explain two distinct ways this sampling method could lead to bias in estimating the proportion of all city adults who shop online weekly, and describe the likely direction of each bias.
Describe a sampling procedure the manager could use instead to obtain a more representative sample, and explain how it addresses the problems identified in part B.

stem: Simulating Free Kick Success: Answer all parts. Show your reasoning and calculations clearly, using standard AP notation and justifying any qualitative claims.
stimulus: A soccer player makes a successful free kick 40% of the time. A coach wants to estimate, via simulation, the probability that the player makes at least 2 of her next 5 free kicks.

part_prompts.text: Describe a complete simulation process using random digits to estimate this probability, including how digits are assigned to represent "made" and "missed" outcomes.

Using the digit assignment from part A (0–3 = made, 4–9 = missed), determine the outcome (number of makes and whether it counts as a success) for each of the following three simulated trials.

Trial 1: 3 8 1 4 6
Trial 2: 7 2 0 9 5
Trial 3: 4 4 2 1 3

Given that 27 out of 50 total simulated trials resulted in at least 2 makes, estimate the probability that the player makes at least 2 of her next 5 free kicks, and interpret this estimate in context.

stem: Warranty Claims Independence: Answer all parts. Show your reasoning and calculations clearly, using standard AP notation and justifying any qualitative claims.
stimulus: For a certain model of laptop, 20% of laptops sold require a warranty repair for the screen, and 15% require a warranty repair for the battery. Records show that 5% of laptops require warranty repairs for both the screen and the battery. Let S = event that a laptop needs a screen repair, and B = event that a laptop needs a battery repair.

part_prompts.text: Calculate the probability that a randomly selected laptop needs a warranty repair for the screen or the battery (or both).
Determine whether events S and B are mutually exclusive. Justify your answer.
Determine whether events S and B are independent. Justify your answer using probability calculations.
Calculate the probability that a laptop needs a battery repair, given that it needs a screen repair.

topic_evidence.title: Introduction to Random Variables and Probability Distributions

stem: Insurance Policy Payout: Answer all parts. Show your reasoning and calculations clearly, using standard AP notation and justifying any qualitative claims.
stimulus: An insurance company sells a 1-year policy that pays out $20,000 if the policyholder files a covered claim, and $0 otherwise. Based on historical data, the probability that a given policyholder files a covered claim in a year is 0.02. Each policy costs the customer $500 per year.

part_prompts.text: Construct the probability distribution table for Y, the amount the insurance company pays out to a single policyholder in a year.

topic_evidence.title: Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable

authored_subtopics: Unit 1: Measures of Center and Spread (Resistance to Skew/Outliers)
stem: Which measure of center and spread is most appropriate to report for this distribution, and why?
stimulus: A researcher records the time (in minutes) that 40 customers spend in a coffee shop. The distribution of times is strongly right-skewed, with a few customers staying much longer than typical. The five-number summary is: Min = 3, Q1 = 8, Median = 12, Q3 = 18, Max = 65.

choices.text: Mean and standard deviation, because they use every data value in the distribution.
Mean and range, because the range captures the full spread including the long visits.
Median and IQR, because they are resistant to the strong right skew and the high outlier.
Median and standard deviation, because the median is resistant but the shape of the distribution doesn't affect measures of spread.

choices.text: It removes the need for random assignment altogether, since sun exposure is already controlled.

topic_evidence.title: Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable

stem: A transit agency records the delay (in minutes) of each of 60 commuter trains in one month. The histogram is strongly right-skewed: most delays are under 10 minutes, but a handful exceed two hours. An analyst wants one measure of center and one measure of spread that will not be distorted by those extreme delays. Which pair should the analyst report, and why?

choices.text: Mean and IQR, because the mean gives the total delay spread evenly across all trains.
Median and range, because the range shows how bad the worst delays were.
Median and IQR, because both depend only on the ordered middle of the data and are not moved by a few very long delays.
Mean and standard deviation, because they take every train's delay into account and so reflect the whole month.

topic_evidence.title: Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable

stem: A school counselor asks 80 teens how many text messages they sent yesterday. The distribution is strongly right-skewed with a five-number summary of: Min = 0, Q1 = 12, Median = 30, Q3 = 66, Max = 410. Which description of typical value and variation is most appropriate?

choices.text: A median of 30 texts and a range of 410 texts, because the range shows the full spread of the data.
A median of 30 texts and an IQR of 36 texts, because the IQR is the distance from the median to Q3.
A median of 30 texts and an IQR of 54 texts, because neither is pulled by the few extremely high counts.
A mean and standard deviation, because they use all 80 reported values.

topic_evidence.title: Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable

stem: A real estate agent reports that for homes sold in one neighborhood last year, the mean sale price was $410,000 and the median sale price was $325,000. A buyer asks for the single value that best represents a typical home price. Which response is best?

choices.text: Report either one, because the mean and median always give the same typical value.
Report the mean of $410,000, because it accounts for every home's sale price.
Report the median of $325,000, because the mean is pulled above the typical home by a few very expensive sales.
Report the mean of $410,000, because the median ignores half of the data.

topic_evidence.title: Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable

stem: Priya scored 83 on a chemistry exam whose scores have mean 74 and standard deviation 6. Marcus scored 68 on a history exam whose scores have mean 61 and standard deviation 4. Which student performed better relative to the other students who took the same exam?

choices.text: Marcus, because his z-score of 1.75 is higher than Priya's z-score of 1.5.
Priya, because her score is about 1.12 times her exam's mean, compared with about 1.11 times for Marcus.
Priya, because she is 9 points above her mean while Marcus is only 7 points above his.
Priya, because her raw score of 83 is higher than Marcus's raw score of 68.

topic_evidence.title: Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable

stem: Lena earns $52,000 at a firm where salaries have mean $45,000 and standard deviation $4,000. Omar earns $61,000 at a different firm where salaries have mean $50,000 and standard deviation $7,000. Relative to the pay at their own firms, who is paid better?

choices.text: Omar, because his salary is 22% above his firm's mean while Lena's is only 16% above hers.
Omar, because he earns $11,000 above his firm's mean while Lena earns only $7,000 above hers.
Omar, because $61,000 is a larger salary than $52,000.
Lena, because her z-score of 1.75 exceeds Omar's z-score of about 1.57.

topic_evidence.title: Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable

stem: Tom scored 35 on a placement test with mean 50 and standard deviation 10. Sue scored 58 on a different placement test with mean 50 and standard deviation 4. Whose result is farther from the typical score on her or his own test, measured in standard deviations?

choices.text: Sue's, because her z-score of 2.0 is larger in absolute value than Tom's z-score of -1.5.
Tom's, because 35 is lower than 58.
Tom's, because he is 15 points from his mean while Sue is only 8 points from hers.
Neither, because Tom's negative z-score of -1.5 shows he performed worse than Sue and the two cannot be compared.

stem: A university health center reports that students who sleep at least 8 hours per night have a higher mean GPA than students who sleep less. The report is based on an email survey in which 320 students chose to respond and reported their own sleep and GPA. Which conclusion is appropriately supported by this study design?

choices.text: Since sleep was not randomly assigned, the survey shows no relationship between sleep and GPA among respondents.
Sleeping at least 8 hours per night causes students to earn higher GPAs.
Because 320 respondents is a large sample, the data show that more sleep causes a higher GPA.
Sleep duration and GPA are associated among these respondents, but a cause-and-effect conclusion is not supported because sleep was not randomly assigned.

stem: A clinic recruits 90 volunteers with mild insomnia and uses a random number generator to assign 45 to drink a new herbal tea nightly and 45 to drink a placebo tea. After four weeks, the tea group fell asleep an average of 12 minutes faster, and a significance test shows this difference is very unlikely to be due to chance alone. Which conclusion is best supported?

choices.text: The tea very likely caused faster sleep onset among these volunteers, because treatments were randomly assigned and the difference is unlikely to be due to chance.
The tea would cause faster sleep onset for all adults with insomnia, because random assignment makes the volunteers representative of them.
Because the participants were volunteers, no cause-and-effect conclusion is possible for anyone in the study.
Because only 90 people took part, no cause-and-effect conclusion can be drawn from this study.

stem: Researchers select a simple random sample of 800 adults from a county and record how many cups of coffee each drinks per day and whether each has been diagnosed with heart disease. Adults who drink 3 or more cups a day have a lower rate of diagnosed heart disease than those who drink fewer. Which conclusion is appropriate?

choices.text: The association cannot be generalized to the county's adults, because coffee drinking was not randomly assigned.
Drinking 3 or more cups of coffee a day lowers the risk of heart disease, because the sample was randomly selected.
Random selection ensures that age, diet, and other variables are balanced between heavy and light coffee drinkers, so differences are due to coffee.
There is an association in the county's adults that can be generalized because of the random sample, but causation cannot be concluded because coffee drinking was not assigned.

stem: A medical team tests whether a new drug lowers systolic blood pressure more than a placebo. They enroll 36 patients, 18 men and 18 women, and randomly assign drug or placebo separately within the men and within the women, instead of randomizing all 36 patients together. What is the main statistical advantage of assigning treatments within each sex?

choices.text: It lets the team conclude the drug works for all adults, since both sexes were included in the trial.
It makes the placebo group unnecessary, because sex differences are already accounted for.
It eliminates confounding from every lurking variable, including ones the team never measured.
It removes blood-pressure variation that is due to sex from the drug-versus-placebo comparison, making a real drug effect easier to detect.

stem: A teacher wants to compare a new study app with textbook review. She has 60 students: 30 in a morning section and 30 in an afternoon section. Within each section she randomly assigns half the students to the app and half to the textbook, rather than randomizing all 60 together. What is the primary benefit of this approach?

choices.text: It allows the teacher to claim cause and effect, which complete randomization of all 60 students would not allow.
It guarantees the class period has no effect on test scores in either treatment group.
It makes the app and textbook groups larger, which gives more data for the comparison.
It accounts for score differences caused by class period, so differences between the two study methods stand out more clearly.

stem: A veterinary researcher compares two diets for weight loss in 24 dogs: 12 small-breed dogs and 12 large-breed dogs. Diet is randomly assigned separately within the small-breed group and within the large-breed group. Compared with randomly assigning diets to all 24 dogs at once, what does this design mainly accomplish?

choices.text: It makes the dogs and owners unaware of which diet each dog receives, so expectations cannot affect results.
It raises the number of dogs in the study from 24 to 48, which strengthens the evidence.
It removes the need for a second diet group because breed size is already being compared.
It controls variation in weight loss that is related to breed size, so a real difference between the diets is easier to detect.

stem: A hospital analyst takes a random sample of n = 60 patients from a very large patient population in which the true readmission rate is p = 0.05. The analyst wants to use a normal approximation for the sampling distribution of the sample proportion who are readmitted. Why is this approximation not appropriate?

choices.text: p = 0.05 is below 0.5, so the sampling distribution of p-hat can only be approximately normal when p is at least 0.5.
The sample size n = 60 is under 100, and a normal approximation needs at least 100 observations whatever the value of p.
np = 60(0.05) = 3, which is less than 10, so the large-counts condition fails and the sampling distribution of p-hat is skewed right.
The true rate p is known, so the sampling distribution of p-hat has no standard deviation to approximate with a normal model.

stem: A botanist plants a random sample of n = 50 seeds from a very large seed lot in which the true germination rate is p = 0.96. Which statement correctly evaluates using a normal approximation for the sampling distribution of the sample proportion that germinate?

choices.text: The approximation is not appropriate, since n(1 − p) = 50(0.04) = 2 is less than 10, which leaves the distribution of p-hat skewed left.
The approximation is appropriate, because n = 50 is at least 30, which is the sample-size requirement for normality.
The approximation is inappropriate because p = 0.96 is greater than 0.5, and normal approximations require p ≤ 0.5.
The approximation is appropriate, because np = 50(0.96) = 48 is at least 10.

stem: A human resources office has 600 employees. It plans to take a simple random sample of n = 80 employees and use a normal model for the sampling distribution of the proportion who support a new schedule, where the true proportion is p = 0.40. Which statement identifies the problem with this plan?

choices.text: There is no problem: np = 32 and n(1 − p) = 48 are both at least 10, so every condition for a normal model is met.
Because p = 0.40 is not close to 0.50, the large-counts condition fails and a normal model cannot be used.
Since 80 is much smaller than 600, the sample is too small relative to the population for the sampling distribution to be normal.
The sample of 80 is more than 10% of the 600 employees (10% of 600 is 60), so the independence (10%) condition is not met.

stem: A random sample of 600 teenagers in a school district is used to build a 90% confidence interval for the proportion of all teenagers in the district who own a laptop. The interval is (0.29, 0.35). Which statement is a correct interpretation?

choices.text: 90% of teenagers in the district own a laptop, give or take 3 percentage points.
There is a 90% probability that a new random sample of 600 teenagers will have a sample proportion between 0.29 and 0.35.
Between 29% and 35% of the 600 sampled teenagers own a laptop, and we are 90% sure of this.
We are 90% confident that the interval from 0.29 to 0.35 captures the proportion of all teenagers in the district who own a laptop.

topic_evidence.title: Justifying a Claim Based on a Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion

stem: A news site reports a 95% confidence interval of (0.53, 0.59) for the proportion of registered voters in a county who favor a school bond, using a random sample of 1,000 voters. Which statement correctly explains what the 95% confidence level means?

choices.text: About 95% of the 1,000 voters in the sample favor the school bond, give or take a few points.
About 95% of intervals built this way from repeated random samples would contain the true proportion.
There is a 5% chance that this sample proportion lies outside the interval from 0.53 to 0.59.
The probability is 0.95 that the true proportion of supporters in the county is exactly 0.56.

topic_evidence.title: Justifying a Claim Based on a Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion

stem: A company surveys a random sample of 1,200 of its customers and computes a 99% confidence interval of (0.72, 0.78) for the proportion of all its customers who are satisfied. Which statement is a correct interpretation of this interval?

choices.text: About 99% of the 1,200 surveyed customers gave a satisfaction rating between 0.72 and 0.78.
We are 99% confident that the true proportion of all the company's customers who are satisfied is between 0.72 and 0.78.
There is a 99% probability that the next customer surveyed will be satisfied.
The true proportion of satisfied customers changes from sample to sample and falls between 0.72 and 0.78 in 99% of samples.

topic_evidence.title: Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable

stem: Monthly rents for apartments listed in a city are strongly right-skewed because a few luxury units cost far more than the rest. A housing researcher wants to describe the typical rent and how much rents vary. Which pair of statistics is most appropriate?

choices.text: Median and range, since the range includes all of the listings.
Mean and IQR, since the IQR is the only resistant spread measure.
Mean and standard deviation, since they are the most commonly used.
Median and IQR, since luxury listings barely affect either one.

topic_evidence.title: Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable

stem: A biologist measures the wingspan of 120 randomly captured adults of one bird species. A histogram is symmetric and mound-shaped with no outliers. Which pair of statistics is most appropriate to describe the center and spread?

choices.text: Mean and SD, since a symmetric distribution without outliers does not distort them.
Mean and range, since the range reports the distance between the two extreme wingspans.
Median and IQR, since they should always be used no matter what shape the data have.
Median and range, since the range is the easiest spread measure to compute.

topic_evidence.title: Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable

stem: The waiting times (in minutes) of 150 patients at an urgent care clinic are strongly right-skewed with five-number summary: Min = 2, Q1 = 10, Median = 14, Q3 = 19, Max = 90. Which pair of values best describes the center and spread of the waiting times?

choices.text: Median = 14 minutes and IQR = 9 minutes, since neither is affected much by the 90-minute wait.
Median = 14 minutes and range = 88 minutes, since the range shows the full spread.
Median = 14 minutes and spread = 17 minutes, since that is the distance from the minimum to Q3.
Median = 14 minutes and spread = 5 minutes, since that is the distance from the median to Q3.

stem: A teacher has 15 quiz scores with a mean of 72. While rechecking, she corrects one score from 64 to 79 and recomputes the mean. How does the mean change?

stem: A data set of 20 commute times (in minutes) has a mean of 55. One entry of 90 minutes is found to be a typing error and is corrected to 50 minutes. What happens to the mean?

It decreases by 40.
It increases by 2, because the size of the change, 40, is divided by 20 values.
It decreases by 2, because the total drops by 40 minutes and is shared among 20 values.

topic_evidence.title: Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable

stem: A set of 8 measurements has a mean of 25. A lab technician replaces one measurement of 10 with a new measurement of 34. How does the mean change?

choices.text: It increases by 3, because the total rises by 24 and there are 8 measurements.
It increases by 24.
It increases by 2.4, because the 24-point change is spread over 10 measurements.

topic_evidence.title: Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable

stem: A quiz has these scores: 5, 6, 6, 7, 8, 9, 9, 52. If the largest score were changed from 52 to 520, which summary would stay exactly the same?

choices.text: The standard deviation, which stays near 16.
The range, which stays at 47.
The mean, which stays at 12.75.
The median, which stays at 7.5.

stem: A technician records the times (in seconds) for 8 lab trials: 12, 14, 15, 15, 16, 18, 19, 30. The 30 was later found to be a typing error for 300. Which statistic would be least affected by this error?

choices.text: The range, because it only involves the two ends of the data.
The standard deviation, because it measures typical deviation from the mean.
The mean, because averaging dilutes one value among eight.
The IQR, which is 4 seconds with either value.

topic_evidence.title: Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable

stem: A teacher's quiz scores are 62, 68, 71, 74, 75, 77, 79 (mean about 72.3, median 74). A late student then turns in a quiz with a score of 3. Which statement about the effect of the new score is correct?

choices.text: Neither the mean nor the median changed, since only one score was added.
The mean and median both fell by about 8.7 points, since both measure center.
The median fell by about 8.7 points while the mean fell only 1.5, since the median is the middle value.
The mean fell by about 8.7 points to 63.6, while the median fell by only 1.5 points to 72.5.

The mean of the 1st and 30th ordered scores.
The 16th ordered score alone, since 30/2 + 1 = 16.

stem: A pediatrician tells a parent that a baby's weight is at the 20th percentile for babies of the same age. What does this mean?

About 20% of babies that age weigh more than this baby.
About 20% of babies that age weigh the same as or less than this baby.
This baby's weight is 20% of the way from the lightest to the heaviest baby.

topic_evidence.title: Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable

stem: An employee at a large company learns that her salary is at the 60th percentile of all salaries at the company. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: About 60% of employees at the company earn her salary or less.
About 60% of employees at the company earn more than she does.
Her salary is 60% of the highest salary at the company.
She has the 60th highest salary among the employees at the company.

topic_evidence.title: Descriptions for One Quantitative Variable Distributions

stem: For the lengths of 200 randomly selected leaves, a botanist reports a mean of 52.4 mm, a median of 52.1 mm, and a standard deviation of 6.0 mm. Which conclusion about the shape is most reasonable?

choices.text: The distribution is right-skewed, since the mean is larger than the median.
The distribution is left-skewed, since the median is close to the mean rather than far above it.
Nothing can be said about shape, since the mean and median describe only center.
The distribution is roughly symmetric, since the mean and median are nearly equal compared to the spread.

topic_evidence.title: Descriptions for One Quantitative Variable Distributions

stem: The commute times of 300 workers have a mean of 38 minutes and a median of 29 minutes. Which description of the distribution is most consistent with these values?

choices.text: Left-skewed, because most workers have commutes shorter than the mean.
Left-skewed, because the mean is greater than the median.
Symmetric, because the mean and median are both measures of center.
Right-skewed, because a few long commutes pull the mean above the median.

topic_evidence.title: Descriptions for One Quantitative Variable Distributions

stem: The ages at which employees at a large company retired form a left-skewed distribution, with a few people retiring in their early forties and most retiring in their sixties. Which statement is most likely true?

choices.text: The mean and median retirement ages are exactly equal.
The mean retirement age is greater than the median retirement age.
The mean retirement age is less than the median retirement age.
The median is pulled further toward the early retirees than the mean is.

stem: A city council wants a simple random sample of 40 residents from a registry listing 2,000 residents. Which procedure best accomplishes this?

choices.text: Interview the first 40 people who walk into city hall on Monday morning.
Take the first 40 residents on the registry, which is sorted by last name.
Number the residents 1 to 2,000 and use a random number generator to draw 40 different numbers.
Mail a survey to all residents and use the first 40 that are returned.

stem: A gym has 250 members and wants feedback from a simple random sample of 25 of them. Which plan is best?

choices.text: Post a sign inviting members to take a survey and use the first 25 who respond.
Ask the 25 members who are nearest the front desk at noon on Tuesday.
Survey the 25 members who visit the gym most often.
Give each member an ID from 1 to 250 and have software pick 25 different IDs at random.

stem: A principal wants a simple random sample of 50 seniors from the 400 students in the senior class. Which method should she use?

choices.text: Select the 50 seniors who have the highest grade point averages.
Number the seniors 1 to 400 and use a random number generator for 50 distinct numbers.
Announce a pizza party and take the first 50 seniors who sign up for it.
Ask each of the 10 homeroom teachers to hand-pick the 5 students they prefer.

stem: A county library system has members who mostly use urban branches, a smaller group who use suburban branches, and only about 8% who use rural branches. The system plans a satisfaction survey of 500 members. Why might a stratified random sample be better than a simple random sample here?

choices.text: It guarantees that the small rural group is included in a planned amount, which a simple random sample could under-represent by chance.
It is the only method in which every library member has the same chance of being selected.
It lets surveyors hand-pick willing members within each branch type, which gives more complete responses.
It removes sampling variability, so the sample percentages will equal the population percentages exactly.

stem: A factory has 300 day-shift, 150 evening-shift, and 50 night-shift workers. A manager wants to compare job satisfaction across the three shifts using a sample of 60 workers. Why might stratified sampling be preferable to a simple random sample of 60?

choices.text: It removes the need to randomize, because the shifts are already natural groups of workers.
It selects entire shifts at random and surveys everyone in them, which saves time and travel.
It guarantees that no selected worker will refuse to answer, so the results are free of nonresponse bias.
Randomly sampling within each shift guarantees that the small night shift appears in the sample, so shifts can be compared.

stem: A pollster will survey 600 voters in a state whose regions differ sharply in their support for a ballot measure, while voters within a region tend to share similar views. Why might sampling randomly within each region give a more precise estimate than a simple random sample of 600?

choices.text: It ensures that every possible group of 600 voters has the same chance of being selected, as in a simple random sample.
The pollster can choose the most typical voters in each region, which makes the sample more precise.
It guarantees that the sample proportion for the state equals the true statewide proportion.
Voters within each region are alike, so sampling within regions reduces variability in the statewide estimate compared with a simple random sample of 600.

stem: Researchers examine the medical records of 500 adults, noting whether each person takes a daily vitamin D supplement and whether the person had a bone fracture in the past five years. The researchers do not tell anyone to start or stop taking supplements. What type of study is this?

choices.text: A single-blind experiment
An observational study
A randomized block experiment
A completely randomized experiment

stem: A teacher lets her 40 students choose either flashcards or practice tests as their study method for a unit, then compares the two groups' scores on the unit exam. What type of study is this?

choices.text: A randomized block design, because the students form two groups.
A randomized experiment, because the teacher compared two study methods.
An observational study, because students chose their own study method instead of being assigned one.
A matched-pairs experiment, because every student took the same exam.

stem: Researchers randomly assign 90 volunteers to one of three diets and measure each volunteer's cholesterol level after eight weeks. What type of study is this?

choices.text: An observational study, because cholesterol was only measured at the end.
A randomized experiment, because the researchers assigned the diets to the volunteers at random.
An observational study, because the volunteers were not a random sample of adults.
A sample survey, because 90 people provided data.

stem: A gardener wants to compare two fertilizers using 24 tomato plants in a garden where half the plants are in full sun and half are in shade, and sunlight strongly affects growth. Which plan uses blocking?

choices.text: Apply fertilizer A to all sun plants and fertilizer B to all shade plants.
Separate the plants into sun and shade groups, then randomly assign fertilizers within each group.
Flip a coin for each plant to choose its fertilizer, ignoring sunlight.
Use only the sun plants and randomly assign the two fertilizers.

stem: Researchers compare two study methods using students whose prior GPAs vary widely, and they place students into 'high GPA' and 'low GPA' blocks before randomly assigning methods within each block. What is the main purpose of blocking here?

choices.text: To remove variation due to prior GPA so method differences are easier to detect.
To remove the need for random assignment of methods to students.
To make sure the sample is representative of every student in the school.
To make sure neither the students nor the graders know which method was used.

stem: To compare two exercise programs, a researcher separates 60 volunteers into a male group and a female group, then within each group uses a random number generator to assign half to Program 1 and half to Program 2. Which description is most accurate?

choices.text: A randomized block experiment, with sex as the blocking variable.
A completely randomized design, since random assignment was used.
A stratified random sample, since subjects were grouped by sex.
An observational study, since sex cannot be assigned.

stem: Public health data show that in months when ice cream sales are higher, more drownings occur. Which of the following is a plausible confounding variable for this association?

choices.text: The year in which the data were recorded, with no link to either quantity
The correlation between the monthly ice cream sales and drownings
Hot weather, which draws more people to swim and also increases ice cream purchases
The number of drownings reported in each month

stem: A school district finds that students who take piano lessons score higher on math tests than students who do not. Which is a plausible confounding variable?

choices.text: The p-value from comparing the math scores of the two groups
Family income, which could affect both lesson enrollment and math scores
The total number of students included in the district study
The average math score earned by the group of students taking lessons

stem: An observational study finds that adults who wear fitness trackers have lower body mass index (BMI), on average, than adults who do not. Which is a plausible confounding variable?

choices.text: Health consciousness, causing people to wear trackers and keep a lower BMI
The test statistic used to compare BMI between the two groups
The BMI values that were measured for the adults in the study
The number of adults who were included in the study sample group

stem: A track coach randomly assigns 24 runners to either a new stretching routine or the usual warm-up, then compares their 5K times at the end of the season. What does random assignment help with most?

choices.text: Making sure the 24 runners are representative of all runners in the league.
Guaranteeing that the two groups have exactly the same mean 5K time before the routines begin.
Keeping the runners from knowing which routine they received.
Making the two groups similar in traits like fitness level, so a time difference can reasonably be attributed to the routine.

stem: A pharmacy randomly assigns 60 volunteers with a mild rash to use either a new cream or the standard cream for two weeks and then rates how much each rash improved. What does random assignment help with most?

choices.text: Ensuring that each cream group contains exactly the same number of men as women.
Tending to balance known and unknown variables, like age and skin sensitivity, across the cream groups.
Removing measurement error from the rash-improvement ratings.
Making sure the volunteers represent all adults who develop rashes.

stem: A software company randomly shows each visitor to its site either layout A or layout B and compares the percent of visitors who sign up for a trial. What does random assignment help with most?

choices.text: Making sure the visitors tested match the company's overall customer base.
Making visitors who see layout A comparable to those who see B, so a difference in sign-up rates can be attributed to the layout.
Ensuring the visitors cannot tell that two layouts are being compared, making the study blind.
Guaranteeing that both layout groups contain exactly the same number of returning customers.

stem: A school district wants to learn parents' opinions about school lunches. It mails questionnaires only to the families listed in the PTA directory. Which bias is most likely?

choices.text: Voluntary response bias, because parents decide whether to fill out the form.
Undercoverage bias, because parents not in the PTA directory have no chance to be selected.
Nonresponse bias, because some mailed questionnaires will not be returned.
No bias, because every questionnaire was sent by the same method.

stem: A radio station asks listeners to call in during a morning show to vote on whether the city should build a new stadium, and it reports the percent of callers in favor. What is the most likely source of bias?

choices.text: No bias, because a large number of listeners will call in.
Voluntary response bias, because only listeners with strong opinions are likely to call.
Placebo effect, because the callers believe their vote matters.
Confounding bias, because a lurking variable is mixed with the stadium vote.

stem: A city randomly selects 1,000 households from a complete list of all households and mails each a survey about recycling. Only 220 households return it. Which bias is most likely?

choices.text: Undercoverage bias, because 780 households are missing from the data.
Response bias, because the survey asked about recycling.
Nonresponse bias, because households that did not reply may differ from those that did.
Convenience sampling bias, because mailed surveys are the cheapest approach.

stem: Students are randomly assigned to use a tutoring app or a traditional workbook. The final tests are scored by a teacher who is not told which students used which method. What is the main benefit of having the scorer blinded?

choices.text: It prevents the scorer's expectations about the app from influencing the scores.
It removes confounding variables such as prior ability.
It prevents the students' expectations from affecting their performance.
It makes the sample representative of all students.

stem: In a study of a headache remedy, a placebo group's pain score improved by an average of 4.1 points, while a no-treatment group's pain score improved by an average of 1.3 points. Using the definition of placebo effect as the difference between the average placebo response and the average no-treatment response, what is the placebo effect?

choices.text: 5.4 points
4.1 points
2.8 points
0 points, because a placebo contains no active ingredient.

stem: Which setup for a trial of a new cholesterol drug is double-blind?

choices.text: Identical-looking capsules coded by pharmacy; neither patients nor the clinicians recording outcomes know assignments.
All patients receive the drug and both patients and clinicians know it.
Patients are unaware of what they receive, but the clinician recording outcomes knows each assignment.
Patients choose between the drug and a placebo, but clinicians do not know who chose which.

stem: A city health department inspects every one of the 312 restaurants in the city. Which term best describes the way these data were collected?

choices.text: A census, because every restaurant in the population was included
A cluster sample, because restaurants are grouped by neighborhood
A systematic sample, because inspectors go through restaurants in street-address order
A convenience sample, because easy-to-reach restaurants were inspected

stem: A company with 1,200 employees emails its satisfaction survey to every employee. What is the best name for this data collection method?

A stratified random sample by department
A voluntary response sample
A simple random sample of 1,200 employees

stem: A zoo veterinarian weighs all 15 giraffes at the zoo to describe the herd. What is this called?

choices.text: A random sample of giraffes
A census of the herd
An experiment
A convenience sample

topic_evidence.title: Independent Events and Unions of Events

stem: At a high school, a student is chosen at random. Let C be the event that the student is in a club and J the event that the student has a part-time job. P(C) = 0.50, P(J) = 0.20, and P(C and J) = 0.15. Are C and J independent?

choices.text: No, because P(C and J) = 0.15 is not equal to P(C) + P(J) = 0.70.
Yes, because P(C or J) = 0.55 is less than 1.
No, because P(C)P(J) = 0.10, which does not equal P(C and J) = 0.15.
Yes, because P(C and J) = 0.15 is smaller than both P(C) and P(J).

topic_evidence.title: Independent Events and Unions of Events

stem: At a school, P(a student rides the bus) = 0.50 and P(a student wears glasses) = 0.20. Among students who ride the bus, 20% wear glasses. Are riding the bus and wearing glasses independent?

choices.text: Yes, because P(glasses | bus) = 0.20 equals P(glasses) = 0.20.
No, because P(glasses | bus) = 0.20 is much smaller than P(bus) = 0.50.
Yes, because P(bus) + P(glasses) = 0.70, which is less than 1.
No, because both events can occur together, with P(bus and glasses) = 0.10 > 0.

topic_evidence.title: Independent Events and Unions of Events

stem: A cafe records 300 orders. Of these, 120 included coffee, 90 included a pastry, and 45 included both. For a randomly chosen order, are 'includes coffee' and 'includes a pastry' independent?

choices.text: No, because 45 does not equal 120 + 90 = 210.
Yes, because 120 + 90 = 210, which is less than the 300 orders.
Yes, because the 45 orders with both are fewer than the 120 or the 90 orders with each item.
No, because P(coffee and pastry) = 45/300 = 0.15, which differs from P(coffee)P(pastry) = 0.40 x 0.30 = 0.12.

stem: For a marketing email, 45% of recipients open the message. Among those who open it, 20% click the link. What is the probability that a randomly selected recipient both opens the email and clicks the link?

A student passes the first exam of a course with probability 0.80. If the student passes the first exam, the probability of passing the second exam is 0.75. What is the probability that the student passes both exams?
In a three-step security check, 50% of travelers pass step 1. Of those, 40% pass step 2. Of those who pass steps 1 and 2, 90% pass step 3. What proportion of all travelers pass all three steps?
At a school carnival, a prize wheel pays $20 with probability 0.15, $5 with probability 0.30, and $0 otherwise. What are a player's expected winnings per spin?
The number of pets X owned by a randomly chosen student has this distribution: P(X = 0) = 0.1, P(X = 1) = 0.4, P(X = 2) = 0.3, P(X = 3) = 0.2. What is the expected value of X?

An insurance company sells a policy for $60. With probability 0.02 it pays a claim of $2,000, and otherwise it pays nothing. What is the company's expected profit per policy, after the claim cost but including the $60 premium?
The probability that a randomly selected bulb from a production line is defective is 0.08. What is the probability that the bulb is not defective?
The probability that a certain flight arrives on time is 0.82. What is the probability that the flight does not arrive on time?
A forecaster says there is a 40% chance of snow tomorrow. What is the probability that it does not snow?
A student is chosen at random from a high school. Event S is that the student is a senior and event F is that the student is a freshman. Are S and F mutually exclusive?

choices.text: Yes, because being a senior and being a freshman are independent events.
No, because P(S) + P(F) is less than 1.
No, because both groups belong to the same school.
Yes, because a student cannot be both a senior and a freshman, so P(S and F) = 0.

stem: A student is chosen at random from a school. Event S is that the student plays on the soccer team and event O is that the student plays in the school orchestra. Are S and O mutually exclusive?

choices.text: No, but only if S and O are independent.
Yes, because P(S and O) must equal P(S)P(O).
Yes, because soccer and orchestra are different activities.
No, because a student can play on the soccer team and also play in the orchestra.

stem: A bag holds marbles of several colors. One marble is drawn at random. The probability it is red is 0.30 and the probability it is blue is 0.45. What is the probability that the marble is red or blue?
Which of the following random variables has a binomial distribution?

choices.text: The number of heads in 15 flips of a fair coin.
The number of flips needed until the first head appears.
The sum of the faces in 10 rolls of a fair die.
The number of hearts in a 5-card hand dealt without replacement from a standard deck.

stem: A quality inspector randomly selects 12 bulbs from a very large shipment, where each bulb is independently defective with probability 0.03. Let X be the number of defective bulbs. Which statement correctly justifies that X is binomial?

choices.text: X is binomial because the defect probability is small.
X is binomial because it takes whole-number values.
There are a fixed 12 trials, each with two outcomes, independent, with constant P(defective) = 0.03.
X is binomial because the sample is large enough for X to be approximately normal.

stem: A teacher randomly picks 6 students one at a time, without replacement, from a class of 20 students (10 girls and 10 boys). Let X be the number of girls selected. Why is X not binomial?

choices.text: The probability of selecting a girl, 0.5, is too large for a binomial model.
Picking without replacement from a small class makes trials dependent, so P(girl) shifts.
The number of picks is not fixed in advance by the teacher.
Each pick has more than two possible outcomes for the student chosen.

stem: At a school, the probability that a randomly selected student takes Spanish is 0.45, the probability the student takes music is 0.30, and the probability the student takes both is 0.10. What is the probability that a randomly selected student takes Spanish or music (or both)?

stem: A 90% confidence interval for a population proportion, based on a random sample of 400 voters, has a margin of error of 0.04. If the pollsters instead sampled 1600 voters, with the same confidence level and about the same sample proportion, what would the margin of error be approximately?

topic_evidence.title: Constructing a Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion

stem: A poll of 500 randomly chosen adults gives a 90% confidence interval for a population proportion. If the pollster keeps the same data but reports a 99% confidence interval, what happens to the margin of error?

choices.text: It gets larger, because the critical value z* increases from about 1.645 to about 2.576.
It stays the same, because the standard error depends only on n and p̂.
It gets smaller, because greater confidence means a more precise estimate.
It gets larger, because 99% confidence needs a larger sample.

topic_evidence.title: Constructing a Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion

stem: A researcher wants a 95% confidence interval for a population proportion with a margin of error no larger than 0.03, and has no prior estimate of the proportion. Using z* = 1.96 and the most conservative p̂ = 0.5, what is the minimum sample size?

A new thermometer is tested thousands of times on liquids with known temperatures. Its readings are tightly clustered, but they average 2.3 degrees above the true temperature no matter how many readings are averaged. What is the main problem?

choices.text: The estimator has high variability, since its readings are not equal to the true temperature.
The readings are not independent, since each is above the true temperature.
The sample sizes are too small, since averaging more readings would remove the error.
The estimator is biased, since its readings are centered above the true value.

stem: In repeated random samples of size 100 from a population with true mean 50, a new estimator has a sampling distribution centered at 56 with a standard deviation of 1.5. Which statement best describes this estimator?

choices.text: It is unbiased with low variability, because its standard deviation is small.
It is biased with high variability, since its values are far from 50.
It is unbiased but has high variability, since it often misses 50.
It is biased but has low variability: its values cluster near 56 instead of 50.

stem: A statistician simulates 2,000 random samples to estimate a true proportion of 0.40. The 2,000 sample proportions average exactly 0.40, but individual values range from 0.25 to 0.55. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: The estimator is unbiased but has high variability: its average is 0.40, yet single estimates are widely spread.
The estimator is unbiased, so increasing the sample size cannot reduce how widely the estimates vary.
The estimator is biased, because many individual estimates differ from the true proportion of 0.40.
The estimator is unbiased with low variability, because its average equals 0.40.

stem: Suppose 30% of all students at a university commute by bike. A random sample of n = 200 students is selected. What is the standard deviation (standard error) of the sampling distribution of the sample proportion of bike commuters?
In a large city, 55% of residents support a new park. A random sample of n = 150 residents is taken. Find the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample proportion in favor.

A factory knows that 12% of its widgets are defective. An inspector randomly selects n = 400 widgets. What is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample proportion of defective widgets?
A significance test of H0: p = 0.5 at α = 0.05 has a 0.32 probability of failing to reject H0 when the true proportion is 0.6. What is the power of the test against p = 0.6?
A researcher tests H0: p = 0.50 against Ha: p > 0.50 with n = 100 and α = 0.05. Which change would increase the power of the test against the true value p = 0.60?

choices.text: Decreasing the sample size to 25.
Increasing the sample size to 400.
Testing against a true value closer to H0, such as 0.52.
Decreasing α to 0.01.

stem: A pharmaceutical company tests H0: the new drug has no effect on blood pressure, against Ha: the drug lowers blood pressure. Which statement correctly describes the power of this test?

choices.text: The probability of failing to reject H0 when the drug does lower blood pressure.
The probability that the drug lowers blood pressure given that H0 was rejected.
The probability of rejecting H0 when the drug has no effect.
The probability of rejecting H0 when the drug really does lower blood pressure by a specific amount.

topic_evidence.title: Setting Up a Test for a Population Proportion

stem: In a random sample of 250 adults, 105 say they use public transit weekly. A researcher wants to know whether the proportion of all adults who use public transit weekly is less than 0.45. Which hypotheses should be tested?

topic_evidence.title: Setting Up a Test for a Population Proportion

stem: A manufacturer says 10% of its chips are defective. In a random sample of 300 chips, 45 are defective. A quality inspector wants to know whether the true defect rate differs from 10%. Which hypotheses are correct?

topic_evidence.title: Setting Up a Test for a Population Proportion

stem: A candidate needs more than 40% of voters to win. In a random sample of 80 voters, 38 support the candidate. The campaign wants to test whether the proportion of all voters supporting the candidate exceeds 40%. Which hypotheses are correct?

Two researchers test the same hypotheses about a population proportion using the same sample size and the same true proportion. Researcher 1 uses a significance level of alpha = 0.10 and Researcher 2 uses alpha = 0.01. Which test has greater power?

choices.text: Researcher 2's test, because a lower Type I error rate also means a lower Type II error rate.
Researcher 1's test, because a larger alpha makes rejecting the null hypothesis easier when it is false.
They have equal power, because both use the same hypotheses and sample size.
Researcher 2's test, because a smaller alpha requires stronger evidence.

stem: Two tests of H0: p = 0.50 vs Ha: p > 0.50 use the same sample size and significance level. In one situation the true proportion is 0.55, and in the other the true proportion is 0.70. Which situation gives the test greater power?

choices.text: They have the same power, because the sample size and alpha are the same.
The situation with true p = 0.55, because it is closer to the null value.
The situation with true p = 0.70, because a larger gap from the null value makes a false null easier to detect.
The situation with true p = 0.55, because power equals the Type I error probability alpha.

stem: A school district tests H0: a new tutoring program does not change mean reading scores against Ha: the program raises mean reading scores. In this setting, what does the power of the test measure for a particular size of improvement?

choices.text: The chance the test rejects H0 when the program has no effect on scores.
The chance the test rejects H0 when the program truly raises scores by that amount.
The chance that the program truly raises reading scores, given the data.
The chance the test fails to reject H0 when the program truly raises scores.

stem: A plant has three machines. Machine A makes 50% of items with a 2% defect rate; Machine B makes 30% with a 3% defect rate; Machine C makes 20% with a 5% defect rate. A randomly selected item is defective. What is the probability it came from Machine B?

choices.text: About 0.030
About 0.300
About 0.009
About 0.310

stem: A school tracks whether students studied and whether they passed. Which expression correctly gives P(studied | passed)?

choices.text: P(studied)P(passed)
P(passed | studied)P(passed)
P(studied) / P(passed | studied)
P(passed | studied)P(studied) / P(passed)

stem: A school surveyed 400 commuters, grouped by mode, and recorded who arrived late this month: Bus 160 (24 late), Bike 100 (15 late), Car 140 (11 late). Among all students who arrived late, what is the probability a randomly chosen late arrival is a bike rider?

stem:
A random sample of students was classified by class year and favorite study method:
Study method: Flash cards | Notes | Videos | Row total
Freshman: 30 | 45 | 25 | 100
Sophomore: 40 | 55 | 45 | 140
Column total: 70 | 100 | 70 | table total 240

choices.text: About 29.2
About 33.3

topic_evidence.title: Carrying Out a Chi-Square Test for Homogeneity or Independence

stem: A chi-square test of independence for 500 survey respondents focuses on one cell. The observed count in that cell is 48, its row total is 200, its column total is 150, and the table total is 500. What is the expected count for this cell?
A basketball player makes each free throw independently with probability 0.3. Let X be the number of free throws made in 4 attempts. What is P(X = 0)?
Each seed in a packet of 6 sprouts independently with probability 0.2. Let X be the number of seeds that sprout. What is P(X = 0)?
A pollster makes 8 independent phone calls. Each call is answered with probability 0.35. Let X be the number of calls that are answered. What is P(X = 0)?
A test of whether a new bus route changes the proportion of on-time arrivals gives p = 0.03 with alpha = 0.05. Which conclusion is correct?

choices.text: Reject H0; there is convincing statistical evidence for the alternative hypothesis at the 0.05 level.
Reject H0, which proves the alternative hypothesis is true.
Fail to reject H0, because 0.03 is smaller than 0.05 and so the evidence is too weak.
Reject H0; the probability that H0 is true is 0.03.

stem: A hospital tests whether a new protocol reduces readmission rates and uses alpha = 0.01. The test gives p = 0.047. Which conclusion is correct?

choices.text: Reject H0, since p = 0.047 is below the common 0.05 cutoff.
Fail to reject H0, which means H0 is true with probability 1 - 0.047 = 0.953.
Fail to reject H0; there is not convincing evidence at the 0.01 level.
Reject H0, since 0.047 is close to 0.01.

stem: A raffle ticket pays $10 with probability 0.5, $20 with probability 0.3, and $30 with probability 0.2. What is the expected payout of a ticket?
In a carnival game, a player wins $5 with probability 0.1, wins $1 with probability 0.3, and loses $2 with probability 0.6. What is the expected net winnings per play?
A random variable X takes values 0, 2, and 5 with P(X = 0) = 0.25 and P(X = 2) = 0.35. What is E(X)?

In a clinical trial, researchers test H0: the new drug has no effect on blood pressure. They conclude the drug lowers blood pressure, but in fact the drug has no effect. Which type of error did they make?

choices.text: Type II error, because the drug was wrongly judged effective
Type I error, because a true null hypothesis was rejected
Sampling bias, because the researchers used a sample
No error, because the conclusion followed from the sample results

stem: A quality inspector tests H0: mu = 500 g for the mean fill of cereal boxes. The machine has actually drifted so that the true mean is not 500 g, but the inspector fails to reject H0. What type of error is this?

choices.text: Type I error, because the machine was not repaired
Type I error, because the inspector reached the wrong conclusion
Type II error, because a false null hypothesis was not rejected
No error, because failing to reject H0 is the safe decision

stem: A researcher tests H0 at significance level alpha = 0.05 and obtains a p-value of 0.03, so H0 is rejected. If H0 is actually true, what is the probability that this testing procedure produces a Type I error?

choices.text: 0.05, which is the significance level alpha
0.97, which is 1 - the p-value
0.03, which is the observed p-value
0.95, which is \(1-\alpha\)

stem: Two researchers test the same hypotheses and the same true parameter value. Study X uses α = 0.10 with n = 400. Study Y uses α = 0.01 with n = 100. Which statement about their power is correct?

choices.text: The studies have equal power, because they test the same hypotheses with the same true parameter value.
Study Y has lower power, because both its smaller α and smaller sample size reduce power.
Study X has lower power, because the larger α makes a Type I error more likely, which reduces power.
Study X has lower power, because a larger sample size increases variability and so makes rejection less likely.

stem: A test of H₀: p = 0.50 versus Hₐ: p > 0.50 uses n = 100 and α = 0.05, and the true proportion is p = 0.60. Which change would increase the power of the test?

choices.text: Increasing the sample size to 400, which reduces the standard error.
Decreasing the sample size to 25, since a smaller sample has fewer chances for error.
Lowering α to 0.01, which makes the test more careful about rejecting.
Using the hypothesized value 0.58 in place of 0.50, so the null is closer to the truth.

stem: A significance test with α = 0.05 has a Type II error probability of 0.35 when the true proportion is 0.60. What is the power of the test against that alternative?

topic_evidence.title: Introducing Statistics: What Can We Learn from Data?

stem: A free-response question describes a school that wants to know whether students who sleep more tend to earn higher quiz scores, and then supplies a table of sleep hours and quiz scores for 30 students. Which first move best reflects how statistics is used to answer a real question?

choices.text: Begin computing the mean and standard deviation of both variables right away, since the table already holds everything needed.
Restate the investigative question in the context of sleep and quiz scores, and keep tying each calculation back to that question.
Ignore the school setting, because context is only decoration and the numbers alone answer the question.
Decide which procedure to use from the sample size of 30, and read the question only after the calculations are done.

topic_evidence.title: The Investigative Question Revisited and Data Collection

stem: Researchers want to investigate whether adults who regularly walk to work have different sleep durations from adults who do not. They enroll adults today and record their usual commuting habits. For the next six months, researchers measure each adult’s sleep duration weekly and compare the two groups. Researchers do not assign commuting methods or ask anyone to change their habits. Which classification and explanation best describe this study?

choices.text: A prospective observational study, because researchers impose no treatment and collect sleep data going forward from enrollment.
A retrospective observational study, because the adults’ commuting habits existed before enrollment.
An experiment, because researchers repeatedly measure the adults’ sleep over six months.
An experiment, because researchers compare adults who walk to work with adults who do not.

stem: A teacher has a numbered roster of 350 students (001 to 350) and wants a simple random sample of 20 students using a random number generator. Which procedure is complete and correct?

choices.text: Generate 20 random numbers with the generator and choose those students from the roster.
Generate three-digit numbers from 001 to 350, skip any repeated number, and continue until 20 different students are chosen.
Generate numbers from 001 to 350 and keep every number produced, even if a student appears twice, until 20 numbers are used.
Pick a random starting student from 1 to 17 and then take every 17th student on the roster.

stem: A marketing team records the three-digit area code of each customer's phone number (for example 212, 415, 305) for 500 customers. How should the variable 'area code' be classified?

choices.text: Quantitative discrete, because area codes are whole numbers, and whole-number values that can be counted are discrete.
Quantitative continuous, because area codes fall anywhere along a number line between 200 and 999 like measurements do.
Quantitative, because the codes are written as numbers and can be sorted from smallest to largest in a list.
Categorical, because each code is a label that places a customer in a group, and arithmetic on the codes has no meaning.
