stem: A survey of 80 students records each student's favorite pet type: dog 32, cat 24, fish 16, other 8. What is the relative frequency of students who chose cat?

topic_evidence.title: Graphical Representations for One Categorical Variable

stem: Two bar charts show favorite music genre. For 200 freshmen, the vertical axis is in counts, and the pop bar has height 60. For 50 seniors, the vertical axis is in percent of seniors, and the pop bar has height 40. Which comparison is valid?

choices.text: A larger share of freshmen prefer pop, because the freshman bar (60) is taller than the senior bar (40).
The same share of each grade prefers pop, because both bars show the pop category.
A larger share of seniors than freshmen prefer pop: 40% of seniors versus 30% of freshmen.
No comparison is possible, because the two grades have different numbers of students.

topic_evidence.title: Graphical Representations for One Quantitative Variable

stem: A histogram of 25 exam scores has bins of width 20 starting at 50. The tallest bar covers scores from 70 up to but not including 90 and has a height of 11. A student claims that at least two students scored exactly 85. What can be concluded?

choices.text: The claim is confirmed, because the tall bar shows that many students earned exactly the same score within that bin.
The claim is false, because the histogram shows that the 11 scores in the tallest bar are spread across the whole interval.
The histogram cannot confirm or refute the claim, because it shows only how many scores fall in 70 to 89; a dotplot or stemplot of the same data would show each value.
The claim can be checked only by redrawing the data as a bar chart, which shows each exact score.

topic_evidence.title: Graphical Representations of Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable

stem: An ordered data set of 11 values is 12, 38, 41, 44, 47, 50, 53, 56, 60, 67, 90, with Q1 = 41 and Q3 = 60. Using the 1.5 × IQR rule for outliers, where does the upper whisker of the boxplot end?

topic_evidence.title: Comparisons of the Distributions for One Quantitative Variable

stem: Maya scored 78 on a test with mean 70 and standard deviation 4. Jon scored 84 on a different test with mean 75 and standard deviation 9. Who performed better relative to the classmates who took the same test?

choices.text: Jon, because his raw score of 84 is higher than 78.
Jon, because he is 9 points above his mean while Maya is only 8 above hers.
Neither, because scores from different tests can be compared only if the tests have the same mean.
Maya, because her z-score of 2.0 is higher than Jon's z-score of 1.0.

topic_evidence.title: Tabular and Graphical Representations for the Distributions of Two Categorical Variables

stem: A segmented bar chart shows, for each of two clubs, the percent of members who prefer online meetings: 40% of Chess Club members and 75% of Art Club members. Which statement can be made from the chart alone?

choices.text: More Art Club members than Chess Club members prefer online meetings.
The two clubs have the same number of members, because each bar is the same total height.
Art Club has more members than Chess Club, because a larger share prefers online meetings.
A greater proportion of Art Club members than Chess Club members prefer online meetings.

stem: SAT-style scores in a large population are approximately normal with mean 500 and standard deviation 100. Approximately what percent of scores are above 700?

topic_evidence.title: Sampling Distributions and the Central Limit Theorem

stem: Delivery times in a large database have a right-skewed population distribution. For a fixed sample size n, consider all possible random samples of n delivery times drawn with replacement from this database. A dotplot places one dot at the mean of each possible sample. The process is then considered for larger sample sizes. Which statement correctly identifies the dotplot’s distribution and describes what the Central Limit Theorem implies as n grows?

choices.text: The dotplot shows the population distribution of delivery times; the Central Limit Theorem makes that population approximately normal as n grows.
The dotplot shows the sampling distribution of the sample mean; its normal approximation improves as n grows, while the population remains right-skewed.
The dotplot shows the distribution of individual delivery times in one sample; the Central Limit Theorem makes those observations approximately normal as n grows.
The dotplot shows the sampling distribution of the sample mean; it must remain strongly right-skewed as n grows because the population is right-skewed.

topic_evidence.title: Summary Statistics for Two Categorical Variables

stem: A school asks 200 students whether they favor an earlier start time. Among 80 juniors, 20 say yes and 60 say no. Among 120 seniors, 60 say yes and 60 say no. Among seniors, what proportion favor the earlier start?

A basketball player makes 70% of her free throws. A student wants to estimate by simulation the probability that she makes at least 3 of her next 4 free throws, using a random digit table with digits 0 to 9. Which design is valid?

choices.text: Let digits 1 to 7 be a made shot and 8 and 9 a miss, skipping 0; one trial is four digits.
Let digits 0 to 6 be a made shot and 7 to 9 a miss; one trial is a single digit; record the percent of made shots.
Let digits 0 to 6 be a made shot and 7 to 9 a miss; one trial is four digits; record whether at least three are made; repeat for many trials.
Let digits 0 to 6 be a made shot, use four digits, but run only four trials and report that proportion.

stem: A bag holds 5 red, 3 blue, and 4 green marbles, and one marble is drawn at random. What is the probability that it is red?
A fair six-sided die is rolled once. Let A be the event that the roll is even, and B the event that the roll is greater than 4. What is P(A or B)?

topic_evidence.title: Introduction to Random Variables and Probability Distributions

stem: The random variable X is the number of late arrivals in a day. The distribution is P(X=0) = 0.15, P(X=1) = 0.30, P(X=3) = 0.20, and P(X=4) = 0.10. The probability for X = 2 is not listed. What is P(X < 3)?
The true proportion of voters who support a measure is p = 0.50. A pollster takes one random sample of 200 voters and gets a sample proportion of 0.44. Which statement is best?

choices.text: The sample proportion is a biased estimator, because the result of 0.44 does not equal the true value of 0.50.
The sampling method must be flawed, because a properly done random sample should give a result of exactly 0.50.
The sample proportion is biased low, and taking a larger random sample of 400 voters would remove that bias.
This is consistent with an unbiased estimator, because unbiased means the center of all possible sample proportions is p, not that every sample hits p.

topic_evidence.title: Constructing a Confidence Interval for the Difference Between Two Population Proportions

stem: In a random sample of 100 customers using app A, 80 are satisfied. In an independent random sample of 100 customers using app B, 50 are satisfied. Which is the 95% confidence interval for p_A − p_B?

topic_evidence.title: Justifying a Claim Based on a Confidence Interval for the Difference Between Two Population Proportions

stem: A 95% confidence interval for p₁ − p₂, the difference in renewal rates between new app users and old app users, is (−0.02, 0.14). Which conclusion is best supported?

choices.text: There is convincing evidence that p₁ is greater than p₂, because most of the interval is positive.
There is not convincing evidence of a difference in renewal rates, because 0 is a plausible value for p₁ − p₂.
There is convincing evidence that the two proportions are equal, because 0 is in the interval.
There is a 95% chance that p₁ − p₂ is between −0.02 and 0.14.

topic_evidence.title: Setting Up a Test for the Difference Between Two Population Proportions

stem: Sample 1 has n₁ = 80 and 48 successes; sample 2 has n₂ = 120 and 60 successes. For a test of H₀: p₁ = p₂, which value of the combined proportion p̂_c belongs in the standard error?

topic_evidence.title: Carrying Out a Test for the Difference Between Two Population Proportions

stem: A random sample of 60 teens includes 45 who own a smartwatch (p̂₁ = 0.75). An independent random sample of 140 adults includes 70 who own one (p̂₂ = 0.50). For H₀: p₁ = p₂ versus Hₐ: p₁ > p₂, what is the test statistic?

topic_evidence.title: Setting Up a Chi-Square Test for Homogeneity or Independence

stem: A researcher randomly selects 300 adults from one city and records each person's age group (18–34, 35–54, 55 and over) and preferred news source (TV, online, print). The counts are displayed in a table. Which chi-square test applies, and why?

choices.text: A test of homogeneity, because the table compares news source across the three age groups.
A two-sample z-test for proportions, because age groups are being compared.
A test of independence, because one random sample was classified on two categorical variables.
A test of homogeneity, because chi-square tests with three rows always test whether distributions are the same.

topic_evidence.title: Carrying Out a Chi-Square Test for Homogeneity or Independence

stem: A random sample of 100 people is classified by two categorical variables. The observed counts are: row 1 has 30 and 20; row 2 has 10 and 40. The expected counts are 20 and 30 in row 1, and 20 and 30 in row 2. What is the chi-square test statistic?

topic_evidence.title: Constructing a Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion

stem: A city planner wants to estimate the proportion of residents who support a new bus line with a 95% confidence interval and a margin of error of no more than 0.03. There is no earlier estimate of the proportion. What is the smallest sample size that guarantees this margin of error? (Use z* = 1.96.)

topic_evidence.title: Setting Up a Test for a Population Proportion

stem: A bottling company claims that 22% of its bottles are underfilled. An inspector suspects the true proportion is different from 22%. In a random sample of 150 bottles, 40 are underfilled. Which pair of hypotheses should the inspector test?

choices.text: H₀: p̂ = 0.22 versus Hₐ: p̂ ≠ 0.22, where p̂ is the proportion underfilled in the sample.
H₀: p = 0.22 versus Hₐ: p > 0.22, where p is the true proportion of underfilled bottles.
H₀: p = 0.22 versus Hₐ: p ≠ 0.22, where p is the true proportion of all bottles that are underfilled.
H₀: p = 0.27 versus Hₐ: p ≠ 0.27, where p is the true proportion of underfilled bottles.

stem: A significance test of H₀: p = 0.30 versus Hₐ: p > 0.30 produces a p-value of 0.03. Which interpretation of the p-value is correct?

choices.text: There is a 3% chance that the null hypothesis H₀ is true, given the sample result.
There is a 97% chance that the alternative hypothesis Hₐ is true, given the sample result.
If the true proportion were 0.30, there would be a 3% chance of getting a sample proportion at least as large as the one observed.
The sample proportion is 3 percentage points above the hypothesized value of 0.30.

topic_evidence.title: Carrying Out a Test for a Population Proportion

stem: A company claims that 30% of customers renew. In a random sample of 150 customers, 60 renew (p̂ = 0.40). For a one-sample z-test of H₀: p = 0.30, what is the test statistic?

topic_evidence.title: Sampling Distributions for the Difference Between Sample Proportions

stem: In population 1, p₁ = 0.60, and in population 2, p₂ = 0.50. Independent random samples of sizes n₁ = 100 and n₂ = 150 are taken. What is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of p̂₁ − p̂₂?

topic_evidence.title: Descriptions for One Quantitative Variable Distributions

stem: Answer all parts of the following question.
stimulus: A teacher records the minutes 9 students spent on a review quiz: 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, and 41. The class is deciding whether the 41-minute value is typical or unusual.

part_prompts.text: Identify the median of the data set.
Describe the shape of the distribution and identify whether there is a potential outlier.
Calculate the mean of the data set and state whether the mean is greater than or less than the median.
Explain how removing the 41-minute value would affect the mean and the standard deviation.

topic_evidence.title: Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable

stem: Answer all parts of the following question.
stimulus: Two classes took different quizzes. On Quiz A, the class mean was 74 and the standard deviation was 8. On Quiz B, the class mean was 52 and the standard deviation was 4. A student scored 86 on Quiz A and 62 on Quiz B.

part_prompts.text: Calculate the student's z-score on Quiz A.
Calculate the student's z-score on Quiz B.
Determine on which quiz the student performed better relative to the class.
Explain why z-scores are useful for comparing scores from different quizzes.

stem: Answer all parts of the following question.
stimulus: A school newspaper wants to estimate the proportion of students who support a later start time. Reporters stand outside the cafeteria at lunch and ask the first 50 students who agree to answer.

part_prompts.text: Identify the sampling method used.
Describe one source of bias in the sample.
Explain how a simple random sample of 50 students could be selected instead.
Explain why the results should not be generalized to all students without caution.

stem: Answer all parts of the following question.
stimulus: A student answers 20 multiple-choice questions on a practice test. Each question has four choices, and the student guesses on every question. The chance of a correct guess on any question is 0.25, and the guesses are independent.

part_prompts.text: Explain why the number of correct answers can be modeled with a binomial random variable.
Calculate the mean number of correct answers.
Calculate the standard deviation of the number of correct answers.
Approximate the probability of getting exactly 5 questions correct.

stem: Answer all parts of the following question.
stimulus: A school fundraiser sells a raffle ticket with the following payoff X: with probability 0.10 the buyer wins 10 dollars, with probability 0.20 the buyer wins 2 dollars, and with probability 0.70 the buyer loses 4 dollars. The payoff is the buyer's net gain in dollars.

part_prompts.text: Calculate the expected value of X.
Calculate the standard deviation of X.
Interpret the expected value in context.
Explain why a positive expected value does not guarantee that one buyer will make money on a single ticket.

stem: Answer all parts of the following question.
stimulus: In a large school district, the true proportion of students who own a bicycle is believed to be p = 0.28. A simple random sample of 400 students is selected and the sample proportion p-hat is recorded.

part_prompts.text: Find the mean of the sampling distribution of p-hat.
Find the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of p-hat.
Explain why a normal model is reasonable for p-hat in this setting.
Explain how the standard deviation would change if the sample size were doubled.

topic_evidence.title: Constructing a Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion

stem: Answer all parts of the following question.
stimulus: A school surveys 120 students about whether they support a later start time. Eighty-four students say yes.

part_prompts.text: State the parameter of interest and calculate p-hat.
Check the conditions for a one-proportion confidence interval.
Calculate a 95% confidence interval for the proportion of all students who support a later start time.
Interpret the interval in context.

topic_evidence.title: Carrying Out a Test for a Population Proportion

stem: Answer all parts of the following question.
stimulus: A principal claims that more than half of students prefer digital homework reminders. In a random sample of 100 students, 62 say they prefer digital reminders.

part_prompts.text: Write the null and alternative hypotheses.
Calculate the test statistic for a one-proportion z test.
Find the approximate p-value and state the decision at alpha = 0.05.
State the conclusion in context.

topic_evidence.title: Carrying Out a Chi-Square Test for Homogeneity or Independence

stem: Answer all parts of the following question.
stimulus:
A school wants to know whether grade level and preference for a new app are independent. The observed counts are:

|           | Likes app | Does not like app |
|-----------|-----------|-------------------|
| Freshman  | 18        | 12                |
| Sophomore | 12        | 18                |

part_prompts.text: Write the null and alternative hypotheses for a chi-square test of independence.
Calculate the expected count for freshmen who like the app.
Calculate the chi-square test statistic.
State the conclusion at alpha = 0.05.

topic_evidence.title: The Investigative Question Revisited and Data Collection

stem: As part of a study of the 40,000 residents of Springfield, researchers randomly survey 500 residents and ask about their income. What is the population and what is the sample?
Explain why random sampling is preferable to convenience sampling for conducting a survey.
